intro: Thérèse Dussaut plays the piano original of Ravel’s Pavane, a stately dance imagined for a princess at the old Spanish court. Its melody keeps returning, each time with more movement beneath its long notes.

sections.label: A · The G-major refrain
sections.mNote: Long melodic notes above evenly spaced quavers

sections.label: B · Distant chords over low B
sections.mNote: Très lointain: a chordal melody over held bass octaves

sections.label: A′ · The refrain over fuller chords
sections.mNote: The first tune returns with a heavier bass

sections.label: C · A soft line after fortissimo
sections.mNote: Subitement très doux et très lié: suddenly soft and connected

sections.label: A″ · The refrain over flowing semiquavers
sections.mNote: Ravel marks the tune clearly above the busier accompaniment

relations.label: The refrain returns
relations.basis: The first return of A follows the contrasting B episode in the work’s A–B–A–C–A design; the later excerpt lies inside the refrain marked near 114 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.925, sustained 25.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 110.5 s (cache/form/ravel-pavane.txt, candidate 4; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

relations.label: The refrain returns for the close
relations.basis: After the broader C episode, the refrain returns again near 244 s. This pair compares the earlier refrain return with the final one, rather than claiming a new theme. CENS diagonal mean 0.954, sustained 27.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 132 s (cache/form/ravel-pavane.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: A long note, small steps
cues.text: The tune holds its first G while the accompaniment takes small, detached steps beneath it. Ravel asks for a soft sound with breadth. The melody can lean across the beat because the accompanying quavers keep walking.
cues.evidence: Demets piano edition, plate E. 623 D., p. 1: opening G, detached quavers and Assez doux, mais d’une sonorité large. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/48/IMSLP384819-PMLP03577-Maurice_Ravel_-_Pavane_pour_une_infante_d%C3%A9funte.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The princess in the salon
cues.text: A real princess stands behind the imaginary one. The Princesse de Polignac commissions the piece and receives its dedication. Fauré, Ravel’s teacher, introduces him to her Paris salon; Ricardo Viñes gives the public première in 1902.
cues.evidence: Bru Zane records the commission, dedication, Fauré’s introduction and Viñes’s première on 5 April 1902 at the Société nationale de musique. https://www.bruzanemediabase.com/en/exploration/works/pavane-infante-defunte-maurice-ravel

cues.title: Distant, above low B
cues.text: Très lointain — very distant. Low B octaves stay beneath a melody in closely spaced chords. The opening’s walking bass has stopped, and the chords move together, quietly, above its held notes.
cues.evidence: Demets piano edition, p. 2: Très lointain, pp, low B octaves and the B-minor chordal melody.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An imagined Spanish court
cues.text: Ravel pictures a pavane that a young princess might have danced at the Spanish court centuries earlier. The title gives this measured dance a vanished dancer. He orchestrates it in 1909, ten years after this piano original.
cues.evidence: Ravel’s explanation of the title: Bru Zane, https://www.bruzanemediabase.com/en/exploration/works/pavane-infante-defunte-maurice-ravel . Orchestration in August 1909 (published 1910): Manuel Cornejo, Ravel chronology (2018), https://boleravel.fr/wp-content/uploads/RAVEL_Chronology_2018.pdf

cues.title: Suddenly soft and connected
cues.text: A broad fortissimo chord gives way to a line marked subitement très doux et très lié. B♭ colours the melody, and little connecting notes fill its gaps. The piano will grow forceful again, but this new episode begins almost under its breath.
cues.evidence: Demets piano edition, pp. 3–4: Large, ff, followed by the sudden soft instruction, B♭ and flowing upper notes.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A busier last refrain
cues.text: The G-major melody returns above flowing semiquavers. Ravel writes marquez le chant: the tune must stand clear of those moving notes. Its long phrases remain recognisable while the accompaniment grows more restless around them.
cues.evidence: Demets piano edition, p. 5: 1er Mouvement, marquez le chant and the refrain’s new semiquaver accompaniment.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The final chord opens out
cues.text: The ending broadens greatly. The last G-major chord is marked fortissimo, with a fermata to hold it: the little dance finishes with the full weight of the piano.
cues.evidence: Demets piano edition, p. 5, last system: En élargissant beaucoup, final ff G-major chord and fermata.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The moving bass rests on B
transitions.to: B · Distant chords over low B
transitions.how: The refrain broadens, then Ravel restores the pace and marks the next phrase Très lointain. Low B octaves hold beneath a B-minor melody in chords. The piano’s bass stops walking; the upper voices now move together above it.
transitions.evidence: Demets piano edition, pp. 1–2: broadening, restored tempo, Très lointain and B-minor chords over low B octaves.

transitions.title: A held chord before the return
transitions.from: B · Distant chords over low B
transitions.to: A′ · The refrain over fuller chords
transitions.how: Chromatic chords slide towards a slower close, and a fermata holds the last chord. Reprenez le mouvement restores the pace and the G-major refrain. Fuller bass chords now accompany the tune, giving the returning melody more weight beneath it.
transitions.evidence: Demets piano edition, pp. 2–3: chromatic closing chords, un peu plus lent, fermata and Reprenez le mouvement.

transitions.title: A strong chord, a soft answer
transitions.from: A′ · The refrain over fuller chords
transitions.to: C · A soft line after fortissimo
transitions.how: The G-major refrain reaches a chord marked Large and fortissimo. A suddenly soft, connected line answers it. B♭ enters the melody, and the bass leaves more space beneath the upper notes. The piano begins to build again from this quiet entrance.
transitions.evidence: Demets piano edition, pp. 3–4: Large, ff, then subitement très doux et très lié and the chromatically inflected melody.

transitions.title: A short bar delays the refrain
transitions.from: C · A soft line after fortissimo
transitions.to: A″ · The refrain over flowing semiquavers
transitions.how: The piano descends through chromatic chords. Ravel writes Très grave, shortens the bar to 2/4 and holds the last chord under a fermata. The G-major refrain then resumes in four beats, its melody above a new semiquaver accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: Demets piano edition, pp. 4–5: descending chords, Très grave, 2/4 bar, fermata and final refrain.

composer.epithet: He made a ballet from two tunes and a snare drum, and gave his war dead a suite of dances.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; Fauré for composition, André Gedalge for counterpoint
Ricardo Viñes · Maurice Delage · Tristan Klingsor · M. D. Calvocoressi
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber and piano music; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: To M. D. Calvocoressi, recalled in his Musicians Gallery (1933)

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery. His mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He kept returning to the Basque coast, and Spain kept returning in his music: the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera that rocks through the Rapsodie espagnole, the clocks ticking in a Toledo shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. Two teachers then understood him: André Gedalge, who gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and Fauré, whose composition class he entered in January 1898. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, became the pianist his music needed. Viñes gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces their composer could never have played with comparable command.
